title_en: Fukushima's 30-Year Tritium Total — Four Chinese Plants Release 60% of It in One Year
excerpt_en: In 2023 Beijing whipped up a nationwide fury over Fukushima's discharge. Almost nobody asked how much tritium China's own coastal plants release each year. The official yearbook has the answer, and it dwarfs Fukushima's cap.
body_en:
When Fukushima began releasing its treated water in 2023, Beijing responded with everything it had: protest after protest from the Foreign Ministry, a blanket ban on Japanese seafood from the customs authority, wall-to-wall coverage in state media, and a nationwide fury online — as if this discharge were about to end the Pacific as we know it. Almost nobody asked a simpler question: how much do China's own nuclear plants release into the sea every year? The data is public. It just never gets announced — or, more precisely, some people would rather you never saw it.

First, meet the main character. Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen with a half-life of 12.3 years. It bonds with water to form tritiated water, and once it is in water, no existing technology can separate it out. Remember that: Fukushima cannot remove tritium, and neither can China's plants. The unit is the TBq — one trillion becquerels. What Japanese sources call a "cho-becquerel" is the same thing.

A String of Plants, All on the Coast, All Discharging

Hongyanhe, Shidao Bay, Haiyang, Tianwan, Qinshan, Sanmen, Ningde, Fuqing, Fangchenggang, Ling'ao, Daya Bay, Yangjiang, Taishan, Changjiang — more than a dozen nuclear plants, built and under construction, and every single one sits on the coast. That is no coincidence: the radioactive liquid waste a plant produces ultimately ends up in the coastal waters next door.

What Gets Released, and How

A nuclear plant discharges radioactivity along two paths:

Liquid effluents (into the sea): Wastewater from the primary circuit and other systems is collected and stored, treated by evaporation, ion exchange and filtration, sampled and tested, then released in batches together with the plant's circulating cooling water into the nearby sea. Tritium accounts for the overwhelming share, followed by carbon-14; other nuclides (cesium, strontium, cobalt and the like) are present at very low levels. China's standard caps the concentration of all nuclides other than tritium and carbon-14 at 1,000 Bq/L for coastal sites.

Gaseous effluents (into the air): Waste gas passes through high-efficiency filters and iodine adsorbers, is held in storage to decay, and is then released through a tall stack. It contains noble gases (krypton, xenon), iodine-131, aerosol particles, carbon-14 and gaseous tritium.

One technical boundary deserves emphasis: evaporation, ion exchange and filtration can strip out most nuclides, but tritium is chemically part of water itself. It cannot be removed — only diluted in large volumes of seawater and released. On this point, China's plants and Fukushima obey exactly the same physics.

The Ledger: How Much Per Year

Start with the allowances. Under the current national standard, GB 6249-2011, a 3,000 MWt light-water reactor may release up to 75 TBq of liquid tritium per year; for a heavy-water reactor the figure is a remarkable 350 TBq. The allowance stacks with every unit on a site — and Qinshan has nine units, two of them heavy-water reactors.

Now the actual releases. The figures below come from the China Nuclear Energy Yearbook (2021, 2022 editions), published by the China Nuclear Energy Association from the plants' own reported data:

Plant20202021
Qinshan (Zhejiang)143 TBq (Plant III only)218 TBq (whole site)
Yangjiang (Guangdong)122 TBq112 TBq
Ningde (Fujian)111 TBq102 TBq
Hongyanhe (Liaoning)107 TBq90 TBq

In 2021 these four plants alone released 522 TBq — and they are only four of more than a dozen. Newer data is no prettier: in 2022 Qinshan alone released 202 TBq, and according to Kyodo News' reading of the 2023 yearbook, 15 of the 19 monitoring points at China's 13 nuclear plants exceeded Fukushima's 22 TBq annual cap.

Side by Side with Fukushima

Fukushima's situation: roughly 1.34 million tonnes of accumulated treated water, containing an estimated 860 TBq of tritium in total (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry estimate). The ALPS system removes 62 nuclides other than tritium and carbon-14, the water is diluted below 1,500 Bq/L, and Japan set itself an annual release cap of 22 TBq, to be discharged over about 30 years. Releases began in August 2023; by November 2026, after more than three years, the cumulative total stood at about 42.9 TBq (TEPCO's official discharge records).

Annual comparison: Fukushima's cap is 22 TBq a year. Qinshan released 218 TBq in one year — nearly ten times the cap. Yangjiang's 112 TBq is about five times; Ningde's 102 TBq about 4.6 times; Hongyanhe's 90 TBq about four times. Even China's own regulatory allowance for a single light-water reactor, 75 TBq a year, is 3.4 times Fukushima's cap.

Total comparison: Fukushima's entire inventory is 860 TBq, to be spread over some 30 years. Four Chinese plants released 522 TBq in a single year — 60 percent of Fukushima's total. In other words, what Fukushima plans to release over three decades, these four plants discharge in under two years. Fukushima's actual releases over three-plus years, 42.9 TBq, amount to less than one fifth of what Qinshan released in 2021 alone.

(Note: Qinshan's 2019 and 2020 figures cover Plant III only; from 2021 they cover the whole site. Fukushima figures are TEPCO's per-round actuals summed by fiscal year. The "four-plant total" is just that — four plants out of more than a dozen nationwide.)

Not Just Tritium: Strontium, Cesium, Cobalt, Carbon-14

Is tritium all that goes into the sea? No. Liquid effluents also carry carbon-14 and a string of other nuclides — strontium-90, cesium-137, cobalt-60 among them — while gaseous effluents carry noble gases and iodine.

Take Qinshan's official 2022 nuclear safety report. That year its liquid effluents contained about 0.016 TBq of carbon-14 (light-water reactors), plus a bundled category of "other nuclides" — strontium-90, cesium-137, cobalt-60 and the rest lumped together — of about 0.78 GBq from the light-water units and 2.6 GBq from the heavy-water units. The air side is worth a look too: about 108 TBq of gaseous tritium (bringing Qinshan's all-pathway tritium total for 2022 to roughly 310 TBq), about 1.56 TBq of gaseous carbon-14 — a full 30 percent of its annual allowance — and about 3.1 TBq of noble gases.

These numbers are orders of magnitude below tritium, but the nuclides are different in character: strontium-90 has a half-life of about 29 years and lodges in bone; cesium-137's half-life is about 30 years. And here is the transparency problem: Chinese plants publish only one bundled "other nuclides" total. How much strontium, how much cesium, individually? The public has no way to find out.

At Fukushima, the ALPS system exists precisely to remove those 62 nuclides, strontium-90 and cesium-137 included, and before every batch TEPCO publishes the "sum of concentration ratios" for all non-tritium nuclides — between 0.08 and 0.61 across batches so far, against a legal limit of 1. Fukushima's real risk lies there too: according to Japan's environment ministry, roughly 70 percent of the stored water did not meet standards after one pass through ALPS and must be re-treated before release. One side publishes a nuclide-by-nuclide list for every batch, for the whole world to inspect. The other offers a single bundled number. Which one inspires more confidence is left as an exercise for the reader.

Incitement on One Side, Concealment on the Other

Everyone remembers how the 2023 outrage was built: press conference after press conference at the Foreign Ministry, a single customs notice suspending all Japanese seafood imports, "nuclear-contaminated water" trending day after day, and a public whipped into righteous fury. Judging by the volume of the condemnation, you would assume China's own nuclear plants were as clean as distilled water.

The reality is otherwise. How much tritium China's plants release each year is locked inside an industry yearbook, published a year late, and never announced to the public. Data after 2022 remains unavailable anywhere. When these figures finally became widely known in 2023, the irony was thick: it was the Japanese Embassy in Beijing that dug out the China Nuclear Energy Yearbook and posted the numbers to rebut China's protests. The discharge ledger of China's own nuclear plants was shown to the Chinese public by foreigners.

And the concealment is tightening. Qinshan used to be the most transparent plant in the country: its annual report carried a complete discharge table — limits and percentages, all there. That is where the 202 TBq figure for 2022 comes from. But I pulled up Qinshan's 2023 annual report and read it: the table has been deleted, wholesale. In its place, one sentence — releases were "below the state-approved annual control values, meeting regulatory requirements." How much was released? You don't get to know. It complied. End of story.

It has happened before. In 2021, when noble-gas levels rose in Taishan's primary circuit after fuel-rod damage, the Chinese public learned about it from CNN first; only afterwards did the National Nuclear Safety Administration confirm that about five fuel rods (out of more than 60,000) had been damaged and that radiation levels outside the plant were normal. The incident itself was minor. The sequence speaks volumes.

To portray 22 TBq a year as a national catastrophe while locking away your own 218 TBq ledger is not environmental protection. It is nuclear safety used as a propaganda weapon: the strictest standards in the world when outrage is needed, and not even a number when the turn comes to your own plants.

Conclusion

This is not a defense of Fukushima. The water there is accident wastewater; whether it should be released at all, and whether ALPS can be trusted, is a separate argument. What is on the table here is one simple fact: if 22 TBq a year justifies nationwide outrage and a ban on Japanese seafood, then the 90 to 218 TBq legally released into China's own coastal waters every year deserve, at the very least, to be publicly known. More than a dozen plants line China's coast, and the seafood market nearest to them may be much closer to you than Fukushima is.

There are two reasons to lay these numbers out. First, so you know what is being discharged outside your own door, and how much. Second, so that the next time someone works you into a fury over 22 TBq, you stop and ask who handed you that anger.

(Sources: China Nuclear Energy Yearbook 2021, 2022, 2023; Embassy of Japan in China, "Q&A on ALPS Treated Water"; TEPCO official discharge records; Qinshan Nuclear Power, Annual Nuclear Safety Disclosure Reports 2022 and 2023; GB 6249-2011, Radiation Protection Regulations for Nuclear Power Plants.)
